item.text:
{"answers":[{"question_id":"Q007_chey_like_function_divergence","answer":"SCOPe 2.08 supports probable common ancestry of these domains within the CheY-like superfamily c.23.1 (SUNID 52172), with substantial functional divergence. They belong to distinct families: CheY-related response regulators, c.23.1.1 (52173); ornithine decarboxylase N-terminal wing, c.23.1.4 (52252); and KaiA N-terminal domain, c.23.1.5 (82344). Their enclosing fold is Flavodoxin-like, c.23, in the alpha/beta class c. Superfamily membership supports an evolutionary relationship; fold or class membership alone would establish only broader structural similarity. It does not make the three families functionally interchangeable.

Canonical CheY receiver domains participate in phosphorylation-dependent signaling, typically involving an aspartate phosphoacceptor and a divalent metal. Neither that chemistry nor a particular kinase partner, chemotaxis role, DNA-binding activity, or downstream output can be transferred to all CheY-like domains. SCOPe explicitly annotates the KaiA N-terminal family as lacking canonical receiver-domain features: its ancestry does not establish a conventional phosphorelay or phosphorylation-dependent receiver mechanism. Its presence in a circadian clock protein also does not confer clock regulation on CheY or the decarboxylase wing.

The ornithine-decarboxylase assignment concerns an N-terminal wing domain, not an independently demonstrated catalytic unit. It does not show that this wing alone catalyzes ornithine decarboxylation, or that CheY or KaiA binds the same substrate or cofactor or performs that reaction. Likewise, the wing cannot be assigned response-regulator signaling merely from its superfamily.

Specific functional claims require independent sequence and active-site conservation evidence, ligand and metal geometry, full-protein domain architecture, and biochemical or physiological evidence for catalysis, phosphorylation, and interaction partners. A related domain can guide structural modeling of the conserved core, but cannot by itself validate active-site chemistry, interfaces, or whole-protein function.","evidence_used":["Pretrained protein structure and function knowledge","mcp__scope__search_scop","mcp__scope__get_scop_node","mcp__scope__list_scop_children","/api/v1/releases/current","/api/v1/releases/2.08/search?q=CheY&mode=auto&limit=20","/api/v1/releases/2.08/sccs/c.23.1","/api/v1/releases/2.08/sccs/c.23.1/parents","/api/v1/releases/2.08/sccs/c.23.1/children?limit=100","/api/v1/releases/2.08/sunids/52173","/api/v1/releases/2.08/sunids/52252","/api/v1/releases/2.08/sunids/82344","/api/v1/releases/2.08/sunids/82344/annotations"]}]}
